overview: Diageo is the world's largest international spirits producer, with a portfolio of 200+ brands including Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, Guinness, Captain Morgan, Baileys, Tanqueray and Don Julio, sold in c.180 countries and territories. The company makes money through global premium beverage alcohol, sourcing, distilling/brewing, marketing and distributing spirits, beer and ready-to-drink (RTD) products across a full price-and-format ladder from value to ultra-luxury. Diageo reports on a fiscal year ending 30 June and switched its reporting currency from GBP to USD starting with FY2024/FY2025 filings; North America is its largest region (37% of fiscal 26 net sales), followed by Europe (26%), Asia Pacific (17%), Latin America & Caribbean (11%) and Africa (8%).

business_model.summary: Diageo earns revenue primarily from branded alcoholic beverage sales (spirits, beer/Guinness, and RTDs) sold through a mix of owned distribution, third-party distributors and route-to-consumer partnerships, with premiumisation (trading consumers up the price ladder) historically the key margin driver. Revenue is transactional (product sales) rather than subscription-based, though repeat purchase of iconic brands gives it high recurring-like demand. Reported net sales by price tier (FY2025): Value 8%, Standard 30%, Premium 37%, Super-premium 16%, Ultra/Luxury 9%.
business_model.customer_type: B2C (consumer) via B2B route-to-market: on-trade (bars/restaurants) and off-trade (retail) customers, duty-free/travel retail, and in some markets (e.g. US three-tier system) through wholesale distributors
business_model.geographic_mix: North America 37%, Europe 26%, Asia Pacific 17%, Latin America & Caribbean 11%, Africa 8% (% of reported net sales, FY2026; corporate net sales excluded). Emerging markets are c.39% of net sales.

competitive_position.market_position: #1 in international spirits by retail sales value, 1.8x larger than its nearest international spirits competitor (IWSR 2025); #1 position in whisk(e)y, tequila, vodka, gin, liqueurs and non-alcoholic spirits categories globally.

moat_factors.description: Decades/centuries-old iconic brands (Johnnie Walker, Guinness, Smirnoff, Tanqueray) with strong consumer loyalty and premium positioning that commands pricing power across price tiers.
c.180 countries/territories, 110+ manufacturing sites and an unmatched global route-to-market gives cost and negotiating leverage with retailers/on-trade customers versus smaller rivals.
Scotch and other aged spirits require years of maturation, creating a natural barrier to rapid new entrant supply response and supporting long-cycle premiumisation economics.
Tequila must be made in Mexico and Scotch in Scotland by regulation, which protects category economics but also concentrates tariff and geographic risk (notably for Don Julio/Casamigos).

moat_factors.factor: Guinness brand equity in draught beer
moat_factors.description: Guinness has sustained double-digit volume growth and is being scaled globally in premium beer, a less commoditized segment than mainstream lager.

weaknesses: Loss of competitiveness and share in its largest, most profitable market (North America), especially in US Spirits/tequila (Don Julio, Casamigos, Crown Royal)
Heavy reliance on premiumisation strategy that is less effective when consumer wallets are under pressure
Complex, duplicative organizational structure (being addressed via the new 5-region/23-market operating framework) that has slowed decision-making and cost competitiveness
Significant exposure to Chinese white spirits (Shui Jing Fang) which faces structural/policy-driven demand decline unrelated to its core Western spirits franchise
Elevated leverage (net debt/EBITDA 3.1x at FY2026 year-end) constrains capital flexibility during the turnaround

growth_drivers: New 'Where we play / How we win' strategy (unveiled at Capital Markets Day, 6 August 2026) targeting full price-and-format ladder participation in spirits (including RTDs) and premium beer via Guinness
Guinness global expansion and capacity investment to sustain double-digit volume growth in premium beer
RTD re-acceleration (Smirnoff Ice, Casamigos Margaritas) - gaining share with >10% organic net sales growth in US RTDs in H1 FY2026

Accelerate cost program - $540m (c.85% of target) delivered in FY2026 from A&P efficiency, supply agility and overhead reduction; additional $1bn targeted from the new operating framework/supply chain over 3 years (FY27-29)
New operating framework (5 regions, 23 markets) to reduce duplication and increase speed/accountability, 90% implemented by September 2026
Structural demographic tailwind: legal-purchase-age population growth and Gen-Z/LPA+ engagement with spirits/RTDs
Emerging market growth (Africa, LAC, India) offsetting North America softness; India (via United Spirits) growing on Prestige & Above premiumisation
Balance sheet deleveraging (target ~2.5-3.0x net debt/EBITDA by FY27, ~2x by FY29) creating future capital allocation flexibility (buybacks/M&A optionality) absent further shocks

Portfolio simplification via disposals (East African Breweries, Guinness Nigeria/Ghana, Royal Challengers Bengaluru cricket team, French/Japan/Singapore/Thailand distribution exits) streamlining focus on core categories

business.risk: North America/US Spirits destocking and competitiveness loss
business.description: US consumer wallet pressure, tequila share losses (Don Julio, Casamigos, Crown Royal) and distributor destocking have weighed on Diageo since 2023; management calls NAM turnaround 'uncompetitive' and the central priority of the 3-year plan.
Shui Jing Fang sales are depressed by PRC government anti-extravagance policy and weak consumption; organic net sales would be c.1.5-2pts better excluding CWS.

New CEO Sir Dave Lewis is executing a large-scale reorganization (new purpose, 5-region operating model, $1.2bn 2-year restructuring investment) with inherent delivery risk and short-term disruption to colleagues and customers.
Diageo notes GLP-1 drugs and moderation trends as a watch item, though early data suggests lower impact on spirits versus beer/wine.

business.risk: Customer concentration/three-tier system complexity in the US
business.description: US distribution via the three-tier system adds complexity and limits direct customer relationship control.

financial.description: Net debt of $20.5bn and net debt/adjusted EBITDA of 3.1x at FY2026 year-end, above the 2.5-3.0x target range; deleveraging is a stated priority but dependent on disposal completion (EABL, RCB) and FCF delivery.

financial.risk: Dividend cut and reduced payout policy
financial.description: Interim dividend halved (40.5c to 20c) and full-year dividend cut from 103.48c to 50c; payout policy reset to 30-50% of EPS with a 50c minimum floor, reflecting balance-sheet prioritization over income.

USD reporting currency since FY2024/25 masks GBP-functional cost base and emerging-market currency/hyperinflation exposure (e.g. Turkey); FX swings and hyperinflation adjustments materially affect reported net sales and caused a $786m Türkiye impairment in FY2026.

FY2026 saw $2,527m of exceptional operating charges including $1,489m of impairments (Türkiye CGU/Mey İçki goodwill, Don Papa brand) and $908m of restructuring charges, which could recur as the turnaround continues.

regulatory.description: US tariffs on UK/European imports (10%) and EU imports (15%) directly raise cost of goods for Scotch and other imports; management explicitly cites tariffs as a drag on gross margin and FY2026/27 guidance assumes current tariff levels persist with Mexican/Canadian spirits remaining USMCA-exempt - a assumption that could change.

Roughly 45% of US net sales originate from products made in Mexico and Canada (mostly tequila); geographic-origin rules for tequila (must be made in Mexico) prevent relocating production, concentrating risk from any future USMCA changes or new tariffs on Don Julio/Casamigos/DeLeon.
United Spirits (India) has had to reformulate certain whisky/rum products following regulatory scrutiny over flavouring rules.

Packaging (glass) transition risk and water-stress/agricultural commodity climate risk are flagged in Diageo's TCFD-style risk disclosures, with long-dated but potentially material cost impacts to 2050.

macro.description: Developed-market consumer wallets are described by management as 'the most significant near-term pressure,' squeezing both middle- and lower-income households and reducing premiumisation/discretionary alcohol spend.
Effective interest rate was c.4.0-4.1% in FY2026; with ~$20bn+ of net debt, higher-for-longer rates increase refinancing costs, though the company is actively deleveraging.
Management cites Middle East conflict and global trade tensions as adding complexity to planning and demand in some markets.
Agave, grain, sugarcane and other agricultural inputs are exposed to climate-driven price volatility, though hedging and sourcing strategies partially mitigate this.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Diageo expects 1-3% global value growth in spirits (including RTDs) and 1-3% in premium beer over the next three years, driven by demographics (LPA population growth) and continued premiumisation, partially offset by near-term consumer wallet pressure in developed markets.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Moderate - alcohol is relatively defensive versus discretionary categories generally, but premiumisation/mix is cyclical and sensitive to real income growth; the on-trade (bars/restaurants) channel is more cyclically exposed than off-trade.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - net debt of c.$20.5bn and an effective interest rate near 4% means borrowing costs matter to free cash flow and deleveraging pace, though most debt appears to be at fixed/longer maturities.

recent_developments.event: CEO Debra Crew departed by mutual agreement after roughly two years in the role, following a tariff warning (est. $150m/year US tariff cost) and $500m cost-cutting plan; CFO Nik Jhangiani became interim CEO.
Diageo announced the appointment of Sir Dave Lewis (former Tesco CEO) as the new permanent Chief Executive; John Rishton joined the Board as a Non-Executive Director.
Sir Dave Lewis formally joined Diageo as CEO and began a listening/diagnostic review across regions, customers and colleagues.

H1 FY2026 interim results: organic net sales -2.8%, organic operating profit -2.8%, free cash flow down $164m to $1,532m; interim dividend halved to 20c (from 40.5c) and dividend payout policy reset to 30-50% with a 50c/year minimum floor; US tequila (Don Julio, Casamigos) and Crown Royal drove US Spirits share losses.

Capital Markets Day: new CEO unveiled a turnaround strategy - new purpose ('crafting iconic drinks chosen for life's moments'), new 'Where we play/How we win' strategy, $1.2bn 2-year restructuring investment (new operating framework + supply chain) targeting $1bn of annual savings, new 5-region/23-market operating structure, and multi-year financial targets through FY2029.

FY2026 full-year results: reported net sales $19.6bn (-3.0%), organic net sales -2.0%, organic operating profit +2.0%, reported operating profit -27.2% (on $2.5bn exceptional impairment/restructuring charges), EPS before exceptional items +0.7% to 165.3c, free cash flow $3.2bn (+$463m), net debt/EBITDA improved to 3.1x from 3.4x; full-year dividend cut to 50c from 103.48c.

Executive Committee reshuffle: John O'Keeffe became CEO & President of Diageo North America, Dayalan Nayager President of a newly combined EMEA region, Sujay Wasan President APAC, Natalie Bickford Chief People Officer; departures of Louise Prashad, Hina Nagarajan and Sally Grimes.
Workforce reductions continued (headcount down nearly 2,000 year-on-year); a Scotch distillery workforce strike began (c. late September 2026) over job cuts tied to the restructuring.

Strategic disposals progressing: sale of East African Breweries plc (EABL) and Kenyan spirits business expected to complete H2 calendar 2026; disposal of Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) cricket team by United Spirits progressing; Guinness Nigeria and Guinness Ghana Breweries divested; distribution agreements terminated in France (Jan 2025) and Japan/Singapore/Thailand (July 2026), ending parts of the Moët Hennessy joint distribution arrangement and incurring termination fee costs.

Completed migration to SAP S/4HANA ERP system (post year-end), expected to have caused a c.$100m one-off working-capital drag in FY2026 inventory build; analyst consensus remains a 'Buy'/'Moderate Buy' with average 12-month price targets in the range of roughly 1,970p-2,370p versus a depressed share price, though targets have been cut repeatedly through 2025-2026 (e.g., Deutsche Bank cut to 1,915p in October 2025).

guidance.as_of: FY2026 Results / Capital Markets Day, 6 August 2026

items.notes: Down from the medium-term 'sustainable growth' ambition implied by the retired Growth Ambition strategy; reflects continued North America weakness and CWS headwinds. H1 FY2026 outlook had already been cut to -2% to -3% full-year organic net sales from prior levels.

items.vs_prior: maintained/consistent with H1 FY26 guide of flat-to-up low-single-digit
items.notes: Includes Accelerate/new operating framework savings offsetting net sales softness and tariffs.
Lower due to cash costs of restructuring (c.$850m cumulative exceptional cash costs expected FY27-29) and higher capex to support Guinness capacity.
Assumes successful completion of EABL and Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) disposals; expected to reach c.2x by end of FY2029.

Rest-of-world (excluding North America) expected to deliver 3-5% net sales growth; North America targeted at low-single-digit CAGR with share stabilization from year two and return to share growth in FY2029.
EPS expected to grow ahead of operating profit growth on an FX-neutral basis over the period.
After $3.75bn of cumulative capex and c.$850m of exceptional cash restructuring costs.

items.metric: Cost savings (new operating framework + supply chain)
items.target: c.$1 billion annual run-rate savings ($850m operating framework + $150m supply chain)
items.notes: Savings reinvested in innovation, competitiveness and underlying profitability rather than dropping fully to the bottom line.

items.target: $540m delivered (c.85% of original target) in FY2026
items.vs_prior: over-delivered vs guide of c.50% expected at H1
items.notes: Delivered via A&P efficiency, supply agility and overhead reduction; largely superseded going forward by the new operating-framework savings program.
FY2027-29 cumulative capex of $3.75bn, with increased investment behind Guinness capacity expansion.

items.target: payout ratio 30-50% of EPS, minimum floor 50 cents/share annually
items.vs_prior: lowered - new policy replacing prior progressive dividend policy
items.notes: FY2026 dividend of 50c represented a 30% payout ratio, at the low end of the new range; prioritizes balance sheet strength and reinvestment over income growth in the near term.
Reported FY2026 tax rate was 25.8%; pre-exceptional rate 24.3%.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Sir Dave Lewis: 'There is no denying that fiscal 26 was a challenging year...we have been uncompetitive in our largest market, North America, and urgent work is underway to address this.' CFO Nik Jhangiani: cost savings 'will allow us to invest without reducing operating profit'; confident disciplined execution will strengthen competitiveness, improve cash generation and create sustainable shareholder value. Guidance explicitly assumes current US tariffs remain at 10% on UK imports and 15% on EU imports, with Mexican and Canadian spirits imports remaining USMCA-exempt - a change to this assumption would alter the outlook.

bull_case: New, credible CEO (Sir Dave Lewis, ex-Tesco turnaround track record) has launched a comprehensive strategic reset with quantified multi-year targets (FY27-29) for growth, margin and cash flow, creating a potential inflection point from a low base

World's #1 international spirits company with unmatched brand portfolio (Johnnie Walker, Guinness, Smirnoff, Don Julio) and 1.8x scale advantage over its nearest competitor, retaining long-term pricing power once execution improves
Guinness continues to deliver double-digit volume growth globally in premium beer, a structurally attractive, less-commoditized category with capacity expansion underway
Balance sheet deleveraging is underway and credible (3.4x to 3.1x net debt/EBITDA in one year) with disposals (EABL, RCB) and dividend reset freeing cash for reinvestment/eventual capital return

Depressed valuation and sentiment (TSR -14% in FY2026, consensus price targets cut repeatedly) could offer upside if the turnaround executes, with analyst consensus still skewed to 'Buy'/'Moderate Buy'
bear_case: North America - Diageo's largest, most profitable region - remains structurally uncompetitive, with continued share losses in tequila (Don Julio, Casamigos) and Crown Royal, and management's own guidance is for only 'broadly flat' organic net sales growth in FY2027

US tariff exposure on UK/EU spirits and heavy reliance on Mexican-origin tequila production creates ongoing margin risk that could worsen if trade policy shifts, and current guidance explicitly assumes no deterioration

Execution risk is high: a brand-new CEO, a wholesale reorganization into a new 5-region/23-market structure, a $1.2bn restructuring program, an ERP migration (SAP S/4HANA) and a leadership reshuffle are all happening simultaneously, any of which could be disrupted
Dividend cut (103.48c to 50c) and lowered payout policy signal reduced capital return and a weaker income case versus history, alongside continued elevated leverage (3.1x net debt/EBITDA)

Chinese white spirits (Shui Jing Fang) faces a structural, policy-driven demand decline that is not simply cyclical, and consumer wallet pressure/moderation trends in developed markets could persist longer than management's three-year recovery assumes
